title: New roles in Orthodoxy
hook: women scholars and leaders in Orthodox settings; the debates continue

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: open doors. Chabad's emissaries, and Abraham running from the tent door to meet three strangers. Did you pull up a chair for someone? Today, a door inside Orthodoxy itself, and an argument about how far it opens. Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

The Talmud tells of a scholar named Rabbi Meir, troubled by some men in his neighborhood who made his life miserable. He prayed that they would die. His wife Beruriah stopped him. Read the psalm again, she said. It asks that sins be ended, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, and then there will be no more wicked people. Rabbi Meir prayed that way, the story says, and they turned. In the pages of the Talmud, a woman corrects a great sage's reading of a verse, and he listens. Today's word is about women taking up roles of learning and leadership in Orthodox life now.
screen: `RABBI MEIR'S PRAYER.` → `BERURIAH: SINS, NOT SINNERS.` → `HE LISTENS.`

segments.voice: New roles in Orthodoxy. Turn it four ways. First, the old voices. The Bible names women who taught and judged. "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." When the scroll of the law was found in the Temple, the king's men went to consult "Huldah the prophetess." And there is Beruriah, a teacher of Torah in the Talmud's own pages. Second, the new study halls. In recent generations, Orthodox women have taken up deep study of Talmud and halakha in their own study halls, the same loud pages and paired learning we met in the Haredi day, and some now teach it at a high level. Third, new roles. One is the yoetzet halakha, a woman trained to advise on the laws of family and marriage that touch very private parts of life, so that women can ask a woman. Others serve congregations as scholars, teachers or spiritual leaders, under titles some communities have chosen carefully. Fourth, the debate, and it is a real one. Some Orthodox rabbis and bodies welcome these roles as faithful to halakha. Others hold that certain roles, especially the title rabbi, cross a line that tradition has kept, and they say so firmly. Both sides argue from the same law and say they are protecting it. This lesson does not settle it. It only notices that the argument is happening inside Orthodoxy, among people who hold halakha binding, which is why it matters so much to them. Beruriah's story is still taught in their study halls. What it means for today is exactly what they debate.
screen: `DEBORAH, HULDAH, BERURIAH.` · `WOMEN'S STUDY HALLS.` · `THE YOETZET HALAKHA.` · `A REAL DEBATE, INSIDE THE LAW.` · then, large: `SHE JUDGED ISRAEL AT THAT TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one role. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the yoetzet halakha: a woman someone can ask a private question of, quietly, and get an answer from the law. Picture the person who comes to her, nervous, and the relief of being able to ask. Then think of a role in your own world that someone stepped into for the first time, maybe your mother, a teacher, you. What did it cost them? What did it open? Hold it gently, without deciding anything. The bell holds the time.
New roles in Orthodoxy. Women as scholars, advisers and leaders in Orthodox settings, from the yoetzet halakha to teachers of Talmud, and a debate about them that continues. Today's word.
Your line: new roles. Today, look up one of these roles and read how its own holders describe it, and how its critics do too. Day one thousand two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: In some Orthodox communities, women study Talmud and halakha at advanced levels, serve as yoatzot halakha advising on family law, and hold teaching or leadership roles, while other Orthodox authorities oppose some of these roles.
